content: The certainty of the evidence was considered low due to indirectness, as lay health-care providers were part of a broader community-based intervention that included additional supportive elements contributing to the intervention's success. Despite this, the Guideline Development Group strongly recommended that trained and supervised lay health-care providers be allowed to distribute antiretroviral therapy (ART) to adults, adolescents, and children living with HIV. This recommendation was based on existing program experiences where trained and supervised community health workers and lay health-care workers successfully provided HIV testing, care, and treatment services. The Guideline Development Group also highlighted examples from the broader health sector where community health workers, with minimal training, were entrusted to deliver curative and preventive care in maternal, newborn, and child health services, malaria diagnosis and treatment, and tuberculosis care. The public health benefits of lay health-care providers distributing antiretroviral drugs include increasing the number of providers to address shortages of facility personnel, reducing congestion at health facilities, and bringing services closer to communities, which supports retention in care. However, if the supply and stock management of antiretroviral drugs are unreliable, the distribution of these drugs by lay personnel outside health facilities could increase the number of distribution sites and potentially exacerbate stock-outs. Notably, neither of the two studies reviewed included individuals with comorbidities or children. The Guideline Development Group advised that the dosage for growing children could be safely adjusted during clinic visits, with maintenance treatment provided at the community level. The costs associated with training and implementing community ART distribution may initially increase. However, studies have reported significant user costs when individuals must travel to centralized health services to collect medication. For example, a study from Uganda found that the cost to beneficiaries receiving hospital-based care was three times higher than for those receiving home-based care. Task sharing has been shown to enhance linkage to care, improve treatment adherence, and help HIV programs address shortages of professional health-care workers. Strengthened relationships between people living with HIV and local communities can empower individuals. In Malawi, community members were hired as pharmacy attendants to pre-package and distribute antiretroviral drugs, which improved the capacity of pharmaceutical services, facilitated visit spacing, reduced waiting times, and decreased the workload of health-care providers at facilities. All providers should be sensitized to the specific needs of various groups living with HIV, including key populations. Initial and ongoing training, mentoring, supportive supervision, and administrative planning have been critical to the success of programs implementing task sharing. Programs adopting these recommendations must establish systems for routine supportive supervision of health-care workers, including lay health-care providers. Implementing task-sharing strategies often requires revising regulatory frameworks and national policies to allow new cadres of health-care workers to perform new tasks. The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends that all health-care workers, including community health workers, be appropriately trained, remunerated, and supervised. Program experience indicates that sustaining health services based solely on volunteerism is challenging. National regulatory bodies, professional associations, and other stakeholders must address the scope of practice, roles, and responsibilities of health-care workers. Relevant curricula for training various community cadres must also be in place. The local supply chain system must account for task-sharing responsibilities and community models of antiretroviral drug delivery to ensure adequate stock. Task sharing of specimen collection and point-of-care testing with non-laboratory personnel should be implemented when professional staffing capacity is limited. This approach is supported by moderate-certainty evidence and is strongly recommended. Since 2016, additional studies have demonstrated the diagnostic accuracy of decentralized and task-shared specimen collection and testing by non-laboratory professionals. Clinical studies have also shown that point-of-care testing by non-laboratory personnel can improve health outcomes, particularly for infant diagnosis and viral load testing. In many settings, trained and supervised lay health-care providers are already conducting HIV testing and collecting blood samples through finger-pricks. WHO strongly recommends that trained and supervised lay health-care providers independently conduct safe and effective HIV testing using rapid diagnostic tests. Access to diagnostic testing and sample collection remains low in many resource-limited settings, particularly in rural areas, due to shortages of skilled laboratory professionals. Task sharing of point-of-care diagnostic testing and sample collection with lower cadres of health-care workers may address these shortages and increase access to testing for key populations who face barriers to traditional health-care services. A systematic review identified 65 studies, primarily diagnostic accuracy studies, with most conducted in Africa. The certainty of the evidence was rated as moderate. Non-laboratory health-care workers performed various point-of-care tests comparably to laboratory professionals. For example, trained nurses conducting cryptococcal antigen lateral flow assays achieved high accuracy and feasibility, potentially accelerating the prophylaxis and treatment of HIV-associated cryptococcal infections. Point-of-care same-day testing significantly reduced the time to deliver test results to caregivers. In all seven studies reviewed, the median time between sample collection and results received by caregivers was zero days for point-of-care testing, compared to a median of 35 days for laboratory-based testing. The proportion of infants living with HIV initiating treatment within 60 days was 90% with point-of-care testing versus 54% with laboratory-based testing. Task sharing of specimen collection and point-of-care testing with non-laboratory personnel was found to be feasible and acceptable. It would save costs by deploying personnel with less training for diagnostic testing and sample collection, although training, supervision, and remuneration of non-laboratory personnel remain critical. Decentralization and task sharing are likely to improve equity by reducing reliance on specialized personnel, which disproportionately benefits urban populations and increases the transport burden on rural populations. Decentralizing specimen collection and testing, including at community-based sites, may increase access to diagnostics, particularly interventions and technologies capable of returning results on the same day or more rapidly than laboratory-based testing. A systematic review found that non-laboratory personnel found preparing dried blood spot specimens for viral load testing to be easy or very easy, with high success rates for finger-prick blood specimen collection. Task sharing also allows for more rational use of higher-level clinical personnel time, as lower-level personnel can perform point-of-care testing effectively.
